title: Indigenous visual systems before colonial rule
source_facts: Scholarly accounts of pre-colonial Ghana describe long-established Akan, Ga, Ewe and related visual languages in gold regalia, stamped and woven cloth, shrine arts, proverbial weights and memorial sculpture. R. S. Rattray's early ethnographic work and subsequent museum catalogues document these as communicative systems rather than "decorative" artefacts alone.
ared_interpretation: ARED frames pre-colonial Ghanaian visual culture as graphic communication: pattern, symbol and form carried authority, memory and social identity before European print arrived on the coast.
historical_significance: Foundation period for adinkra, kente, goldweights, nsodie and related systems that later interact with colonial and post-independence design.
primary_source_name: R. S. Rattray, Ashanti (1923) — via Internet Archive
evidence_summary: Historical entry compiled 2026-07-05 from cited published sources.

title: Coastal contact and transcultural visual exchange
period_label: Coastal contact and transcultural exchange, c. 1471–1874
visual_system_label: Print, colonial rule and public culture
source_facts: European fortifications and trade on the Gold Coast from the late 15th century introduced new materials, pictorial forms and literacy alongside existing African visual systems. Castle signage, trade documents, religious prints and imported goods entered local visual economies documented in coastal histories and museum collections.
ared_interpretation: This period is not merely 'pre-colonial background' but an active era of visual translation between Atlantic trade, mission activity and indigenous makers.
primary_source_name: UNESCO World Heritage — Forts and Castles, Volta, Greater Accra

title: Colonial print culture and institutional design
visual_system_label: Print, colonial rule and public culture
source_facts: Formal British colonial administration after 1874 expanded government printing, missionary publishing, commercial advertising and vernacular literacy. Gold Coast newspapers, schoolbooks, postage, currency and railway publicity created new public graphic formats documented in national archives and library collections.
ared_interpretation: Colonial print did not replace indigenous visual systems; it layered bureaucratic, missionary and commercial genres onto existing cloth, proverb and performance cultures.

title: Anticolonial and independence visual culture
source_facts: Ghana's independence movement mobilised photography, posters, newspapers, flags, stamps and public ceremony as political communication. Kwame Nkrumah's Convention People's Party and allied cultural workers produced a recognisable independence-era visual field documented in national histories and museum holdings.
ared_interpretation: Independence was visually staged: new symbols, portraits and campaign graphics turned political aspiration into designed public culture.

title: Post-independence public and popular graphics
source_facts: After 1966 Ghana saw changing state media, commercial advertising, record sleeves, cinema publicity, festival arts and workshop-based design education. Photographers, sign painters and state printers shaped everyday visual life in Accra, Kumasi, Takoradi and regional towns.
ared_interpretation: Popular graphics in this era include both state-sponsored modernisation imagery and grassroots sign, music and market visual cultures.

title: Democratic, digital and diasporic design since 1992
source_facts: Ghana's return to multi-party democracy coincided with expanded commercial branding, broadcast graphics, digital media, street art festivals and diasporic design networks. Contemporary Ghanaian designers work across Accra, Kumasi, London and global platforms.
ared_interpretation: Recent Ghanaian design is simultaneously local, pan-African and global — shaped by social media, festivals and international art markets.

title: Adinkra stamped cloth tradition
date_display: documented from at least 19th century; older origins debated
community_or_culture: Akan peoples; associated with Bono and Asante histories
medium: cotton cloth; carved calabash stamps; adinkra dye
source_facts: Adinkra is an Akan cloth tradition stamped with symbolic motifs, historically associated with funerary and ceremonial use. Named symbols such as Gye Nyame are documented in Akan scholarship and widely reproduced in later Ghanaian graphic design. UNESCO and Ghanaian cultural agencies describe adinkra as intangible heritage linked to Bono origins.
ared_interpretation: Adinkra functions as a proto-graphic system: repeatable symbols with proverbial meanings, later adapted into logos, typography and national branding.
historical_significance: One of Ghana's most exported visual languages into contemporary design and diaspora identity graphics.
primary_source_name: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage — Adinkra (related Akan traditions)
evidence_summary: Historical entry compiled 2026-07-05 from cited published sources.
uncertainties: exact origin dates and individual early makers often unrecorded

title: Kente woven cloth as pattern communication
source_facts: Kente is a strip-woven prestige cloth associated especially with Asante and Ewe makers. Named patterns carry social meaning and are worn at ceremonies of status. Ghanaian museums, Bonwire community accounts and textile scholarship document kente as a coded visual language rather than purely decorative cloth.
ared_interpretation: Kente patterns operate like a designed vocabulary of colour and motif — a wearable graphic system central to Ghanaian public ceremony.
primary_source_name: Bonwire Kente Museum / Ghana tourism documentation

title: Akan goldweights (abrammuo) as proverbial graphic forms
period_label: Coastal contact and transcultural exchange, c. 1471–1874
source_facts: Akan goldweights were used in trade measurement and cast or modelled in figurative and geometric forms referencing proverbs and social concepts. Major museums including the British Museum and Metropolitan Museum hold extensive Ghana-related goldweight collections with accession documentation.
ared_interpretation: Goldweights are miniature designed objects: visual shorthand for proverb, satire and authority within Akan communicative culture.

title: Nsodie (memorial terracotta heads)
period_label: Coastal contact and transcultural exchange, c. 1471–1874
source_facts: Nsodie are Akan memorial heads placed at sacred burial sites to honour the dead. Terracotta examples are documented in Ghana and in museum collections worldwide. Met and Cleveland Museum accession records describe culture, medium and regional attribution.
ared_interpretation: Memorial heads embody designed presence — portraiture without individual likeness conventions of European print portraiture.

title: Fante Asafo company flags (frankaa)
period_label: Coastal contact and transcultural exchange, c. 1471–1874
source_facts: Asafo flags belong to Fante military companies (asafo) along Ghana's coast. Flags combine figurative appliqué, proverb and company identity. Collections at the Fowler Museum, Brooklyn Museum and Ghanaian community archives document their role in public performance and rivalry.
ared_interpretation: Asafo flags are a major Ghanaian graphic genre: designed cloth banners for collective identity, satire and historical narrative.

title: Ga mfrankaa (posuban shrine banners)
period_label: Coastal contact and transcultural exchange, c. 1471–1874
source_facts: Ga posuban (military/shrine posts) and associated banners (mfrankaa) combine figurative painting and cloth in urban Accra neighbourhoods. Ethnographic and community documentation describe them as public religious and historical graphics.
ared_interpretation: Ga shrine banners share coastal Ghana's tradition of designed cloth as public narrative — parallel to Asafo but within Ga religious urbanism.

title: Ewe kente and woven identity
period_label: Coastal contact and transcultural exchange, c. 1471–1874

title: National flag of Ghana
source_facts: Ghana's flag — red, gold and green horizontal stripes with a black star — was adopted at independence in 1957. Ghanaian and international sources credit artist Theodosia Okoh with the design. The black star references Marcus Garvey's Black Star Line and Ghana's leadership in African independence.
ared_interpretation: The flag is Ghana's foundational republic graphic: colour symbolism and star motif reused across stamps, coins, sports kits and diaspora identity design.
historical_significance: Primary national symbol of the first sub-Saharan African colony to achieve independence.

title: Coat of arms of Ghana
source_facts: Ghana's coat of arms was adopted on 4 March 1957, featuring a shield with cross, castle, cocoa tree and mine, supported by eagles and bearing the motto FREEDOM AND JUSTICE. Artist Nii Amon Kotei is widely documented as principal designer among a committee of artists.
ared_interpretation: The coat of arms codified resource and history imagery into a single official pictogram used on documents, currency and state architecture.
